items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Goldman (Pasquariello)
items.title: Goldman's AI winners-vs-losers basket has given back its entire H1 gain while S&P ex-AI makes new highs
items.idea: Pasquariello: primary bull trend intact but the easy money is made. Earnings growth peaked, forward upgrades slowing. Goldman's AI beneficiaries vs AI at-risk trade has surrendered its extraordinary first-half gains, and the S&P 500 excluding AI keeps printing new highs. The market has stopped paying for AI exposure indiscriminately.
items.angle: The AI factor is decoupling from the index: leadership rotated, not collapsed. Matters for how I hedge index beta with AI single names.
items.tweetA: The AI long/short basket round-tripped its whole first half. The S&P ex-AI is at new highs. So the index isn't being held up by AI anymore, it's being held up by everything AI was supposed to kill. That's a very different bull market than the one you're positioned for.
items.tweetB: Funny detail: if 'AI winners minus AI losers' is flat YTD, the market is saying disruption is a wash, not a one-way trade. Either the losers aren't dying or the winners aren't earning their capex. Pick one.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Goldman (Pasquariello)
items.title: Apple is now negatively correlated with the Nasdaq 100; S&P can fall with 80% of members up
items.idea: Pasquariello flags extreme dispersion under the index: Apple has turned negatively correlated to NDX, and the S&P 500 has fallen on days when about 80% of constituents advanced. Single-stock vol is huge while the headline moves are mechanical, which makes aggressive positioning hard.
items.angle: Index-level hedges are mis-specified when the top 5 weights drive the tape. Dispersion trades and equal-weight vs cap-weight spread are the cleaner expression.
items.tweetA: S&P down on a day 80% of its stocks went up. Apple negatively correlated to the NDX. This isn't a market, it's five positions wearing an index costume. If your hedge is SPY puts you're hedging the wrong thing.
items.tweetB: Equal-weight S&P +4.9% in October, Nasdaq -6.7%. Same month, same 'market'. Breadth is the real story and the index level is hiding it. $RSP vs $QQQ is the pair nobody is trading.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Goldman (Mark Wilson)
items.title: Google Cloud + AWS report ~$1.1T of contracted backlog, yet the stocks are being sold
items.idea: Mark Wilson stays constructive: Google Cloud and AWS together carry roughly $1.1 trillion of contracted revenue backlog and cloud growth is accelerating, with better monetisation evidence. His thesis is that wreckage creates the entry point; Wall Street is separating AI success from the price paid for it.
items.angle: Backlog is a promise, not revenue. Pair with Alphabet FCF of -$9.1B in Q3: the contract book is being financed by the balance sheet.
items.tweetA: $1.1T of cloud backlog and the market still sells the hyperscalers. Because backlog is the other side of someone's capex promise. Ask who on the other side of those contracts has the cash flow to honour them.
items.tweetB: Cloud revenue doubling to $30.7B at Google and the stock reacts to search. The market is valuing the old franchise's decay faster than the new one's growth. That's a multiple-compression trade, not a demand problem.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Goldman Sachs research
items.title: AI-displaced workers: +1 month to find work, +10pp still unemployed after a year, 3/4 land in equally exposed jobs
items.idea: Goldman finds workers most likely displaced by AI take about a month longer to get re-employed and are ~10pp more likely to be jobless a year later. Nearly three-quarters of recently displaced workers in the highest AI-risk group moved into occupations with similar or greater AI exposure. Technological displacement has historically clustered around recessions, with lasting real earnings losses for older, less-educated, long-tenured workers.
items.angle: The labor shock is a recession accelerant, not a standalone event. It shifts the consumer-credit and wage-growth tail risk toward the next downturn.
items.tweetA: Three out of four displaced high-AI-risk workers got re-hired into jobs just as exposed. They didn't escape, they queued for the next round. Combine that with displacement clustering in recessions and the next downturn does the automation work for the boardroom.
items.tweetB: One extra month of unemployment and +10pp still jobless at 12 months is a rounding error in the payrolls print and a catastrophe in the consumer credit book. Delinquencies will show it before BLS does.

items.title: 'The generals are last to get shot': Mag 7 breakdown, desk went to cash two weeks ago on a SPX/QQQ topping pattern
items.idea: MktContext timer is Bearish. A major breakdown in the Mag 7, which had been buttressing the S&P and Nasdaq, is read as a bad omen. They sold a large portion of the portfolio to cash two weeks ago on a topping pattern. Next test: whether non-AI stocks hold and whether defensive sectors break their uptrends. Rest is paywalled.
items.angle: Sets the counter-case to ChartStorm's seasonal bullishness. Key tell is breadth plus defensives, not the Mag 7 itself.
items.tweetA: Mag 7 cracked and non-AI is still at highs. That is either the healthiest rotation of the year or the last leg before the generals drag the troops down. The tell is whether defensives break uptrend. I'd watch $XLU and $XLP, not $NVDA.
items.tweetB: Everyone's arguing whether this is a dip. Nobody's asking who's left to buy. Passive flows, buybacks and retail already own the Mag 7. When the marginal buyer is the index itself, the exit has no bid.

items.title: Alphabet's innovator's dilemma in numbers: fastest query growth in 5 years, Search growth down to 12% from 17%
items.idea: Q3 Search revenue +12% to $63.4B vs +17% prior quarter, even as query growth hit a five-year high. Management admits lower AI Mode monetisation drove the slowdown. Google Cloud doubled to $30.7B, Gemini has 1B users, capex guide is $195-205B for 2026 with a bigger step-up in 2027, and Q3 FCF was -$9.1B on $42.3B operating cash flow.
items.angle: Revenue per query is the metric. If AI answers cut RPM, every extra query is a margin dilution. Alphabet is now a negative-FCF company funding its own disruption.
items.tweetA: Query growth: fastest in 5 years. Search revenue growth: 17% to 12%. More usage, less money per use. That's the cleanest evidence yet that AI answers deflate ad yield. $GOOGL is paying $200B of capex to shrink its own monetisation rate.
items.tweetB: Operating cash flow $42.3B. Free cash flow -$9.1B. The most profitable ad machine in history is now cash negative and calling it a strategy. At what RPM does AI Mode break even versus classic search? Nobody has given the number.

items.title: Intel -28.6% on Q4 guide: EPS $0.25 vs $0.44, client revenue down 20%+ QoQ, PC shipments -25-30%
items.idea: Intel guided Q4 revenue $15-16B vs ~$17.1B consensus and adjusted EPS $0.25 vs $0.44. Client revenue is expected to fall more than 20% sequentially; BofA cites PC shipments down 25-30% QoQ and inventory correction into 1H27, with higher memory costs raising system prices. Data center is up mid-teens QoQ but capped by advanced substrate shortages; an Israel disruption costs ~$300M. BofA cut to Neutral, PT $100 from $145.
items.angle: Memory shortage is now a demand destroyer in PCs. The AI memory bid is crowding out consumer devices, with Intel the first big casualty.
items.tweetA: The AI trade just collided with the PC. Memory is so scarce that it prices PCs out of the market, and Intel's client revenue guide is -20% QoQ. The same HBM and DRAM boom that lifts $MU is a tax on every laptop. Intel is the first bill.
items.tweetB: Server CPU demand is strong, Intel can't ship it because packaging substrates are short. Demand exists, supply doesn't. That's a pricing power story for whoever owns the bottleneck, and it isn't Intel.

items.title: SMH -7% in a day: Intel read-through hits AMD -10.9%, TSMC -6%, ASML -6.5%, memory names
items.idea: The Philadelphia semi index dropped sharply on Intel's outlook and Amazon's capex worry. AMD fell 10.88% in sympathy, TSM -5.95%, ASML -6.55%, and memory makers (Sandisk, WDC, Seagate, Micron) were hit. SPY -1.77%. Eaton -6% pre-print and Trane -4.9% on lumpy data-center bookings hint the power-equipment leg is fragile too.
items.angle: The market treated one PC-heavy name as a verdict on the whole stack. Check whether the datacenter order books actually changed.
items.tweetA: One Intel guide took out $AMD, $TSM, $ASML and every memory name in a day. That's not fundamental information, that's crowded positioning discovering it has one door. SMH -7% on a PC print tells you how much leverage sits in the AI complex.
items.tweetB: $TT cites lumpy data-center bookings, $ETN sold ahead of earnings, $INTC says substrates are the constraint. Three different supply-chain tells in 24 hours. Cooling and power are the next pressure point if hyperscaler capex gets trimmed.

items.title: Marvell in advanced talks to buy Lumentum in an all-stock deal; $MRVL -10%
items.idea: Reports say Marvell is nearing an all-stock acquisition of Lumentum. Investors balked at dilution and execution risk on buying a much smaller but still very large optical-components supplier. Marvell closed at $196.40, -10%.
items.angle: Optics consolidation: custom silicon vendors want control of the photonics layer. Dilution reaction says buyers are not being paid for the vertical integration yet.
items.tweetA: Marvell wants to own the laser. All-stock for Lumentum, and the market sells $MRVL 10% because it sees dilution rather than control of the AI optical bottleneck. If photonics is the choke point, the acquirer should rally. It didn't.
items.tweetB: When an AI-semis acquirer gets punished for buying an optical supplier at full price, it tells you the price of the target already discounts perfection. Who sells next: the laser makers or the people who need them?

items.title: Reddit -29%: search referrals falling faster, logged-in-only test spooks the market despite strong ad profit
items.idea: Reddit fell 29.22% to $91.73 after disclosing accelerating declines in search referrals and warning weaker search traffic could pressure user growth. A plan to test logged-in-only access raised fears of cutting reach and ad inventory, even with strong ad revenue and profitability.
items.angle: Google's AI answers are cutting the top of the funnel for UGC platforms. Same mechanism hitting Alphabet's own RPM from the other side.
items.tweetA: Reddit's problem and Alphabet's problem are the same chart from two sides. AI Overviews answer the question, nobody clicks, the UGC site loses its search referral, the ad slot dries up. $RDDT -29% is what disintermediation looks like when it prints.
items.tweetB: Logged-in-only is a confession: the open web is no longer a growth channel, so you wall the garden. Every content platform that relied on Google traffic is going to run this playbook within a year.

items.title: Roblox -18%: DAU, hours and bookings all declining, younger US users hard to monetize
items.idea: Roblox beat prior guidance on revenue and bookings but showed declines in daily active users, hours engaged and bookings, with younger US users difficult to monetize. Q4 outlook calls for another bookings decline and seasonally lower DAU. Stock -18.05% to $42.99.
items.angle: Kids' screen time is shifting to somewhere else (AI chat, short video?) and platform safety rules are reducing the funnel. Attention economy share loss.
items.tweetA: Roblox lost users, hours AND bookings in the same quarter. That's not a monetization miss, that's a share-of-attention loss in the one demographic that grows up to be every future consumer. Where did the kid hours go?
items.tweetB: Beat on revenue, -18% on the stock. When engagement metrics fall faster than the accounting, the market prices the cohort, not the quarter. Same pattern as Reddit the same day.

items.title: Coinbase -10.6%: revenue miss on soft trading volumes, compounded by Binance breach
items.idea: Coinbase missed revenue as softer crypto trading pressured transaction and subscription revenue. The selloff was amplified by Bitcoin's decline after Binance's reported security breach, which hit crypto-exposed equities broadly. Stock closed at $143.54.
items.angle: Equity market priced the hack as a sector-wide trust hit within hours; on-chain price reaction was smaller than the equity reaction.
items.tweetA: Coinbase missed on volumes in the same session Binance got drained of $6.3B. Whether it's trust leaving centralized venues or just volume drought, $COIN is the cleanest liquid proxy for crypto retail participation. It says participation is shrinking.
items.tweetB: A $6.3B hack at the biggest exchange and the largest US exchange stock falls 10%. If the contagion trade is 'users move to regulated custody', why isn't $COIN up?

items.title: Global Payments +13% on ~$40B take-private chatter; ICE enters perpetual markets; Cboe prints record 0DTE
items.idea: FT reported CD&R and GTCR are pursuing a take-private of Global Payments valued around $40B including debt. Separately ICE announced a partnership to enter perpetual markets, and Cboe beat with record 0DTE trading and raised its organic growth outlook while cutting opex guidance.
items.angle: Perps are migrating from crypto into traditional exchange infrastructure. 0DTE record volume is a retail and vol-selling gamma story.
items.tweetA: ICE going into perpetual markets is the quietest big story of the week. Perps were crypto's native product, now the NYSE parent wants a piece. Same week Cboe prints record 0DTE. The exchange business is converging on never-expiring leverage.
items.tweetB: PE circling a $40B payments processor while Binance loses $6.3B in one night. Legacy payment rails with captive merchants are cheap; crypto rails with security risk are not. Capital is voting on which plumbing it trusts.

items.title: Spotify +6.5% on report of an AI music-remix tier for early 2027 with Universal, Merlin and Believe signed
items.idea: Spotify is reportedly preparing an AI remix service for early 2027 at an extra monthly fee. Licensing is already agreed with Universal Music, Merlin and Believe; talks continue with Sony and Warner.
items.angle: Labels licensing generative remix is a regime change from litigation to rev-share. New ARPU lever for audio platforms.
items.tweetA: Labels spent two years suing AI music companies. Now Universal, Merlin and Believe are licensing remixing to Spotify for a surcharge. Litigation was the opening bid. The prize is a second subscription on top of the first.
items.tweetB: If remix becomes a paid tier, the unit economics of a song change: every track is a base layer, not a finished product. Who owns the stems owns the royalties.

items.title: Late-cycle tells: Stryker cuts outlook, Trane trims margin guide, T. Rowe posts $28.3B outflows
items.idea: Stryker missed and cut growth citing weaker hip and knee procedures plus a Peripheral Vascular goodwill impairment. Trane cut incremental margin guidance on supply-chain costs and weaker bookings. T. Rowe Price reported $28.3B net client outflows. Against that, Regeneron, T-Mobile, ICE and Mondelez (lower cocoa costs) beat.
items.angle: Dispersion within earnings season: cyclical industrials and medtech wobble while defensives and cost-deflation names win. Cocoa relief is real.
items.tweetA: Stryker cuts on weaker joint procedures, Trane on supply-chain costs, T. Rowe bleeding $28B in a quarter. Each is a different sector telling you the same thing: volume is softening and cost pass-through is running out of runway.
items.tweetB: Mondelez rallying on lower cocoa is the quiet reflation reversal. Input costs deflating in food while memory and substrates inflate in tech. The CPI basket and the capex basket are moving in opposite directions.

items.title: FMC +30.5% on channel-inventory reset: new rebate model, price cuts in Brazil, Argentina, US, Canada
items.idea: FMC surged after detailing steps to clear elevated channel inventory: a new North American pricing-and-rebate model and price cuts on higher-priced products in four countries. Management says the reset supports recovery in 2027.
items.angle: Agrochemical destocking cycle may be ending after generic price pressure; farm input demand inflection signal.
items.tweetA: FMC +30% for cutting prices. Markets pay up when a company finally clears the channel instead of hiding inventory. Agchem destocking has run for two years. A capitulation print is how bottoms look, not how they feel.
items.tweetB: Cutting prices in Brazil, Argentina, the US and Canada at once means generics won the pricing war. The recovery thesis needs farmer margins to follow. Soybean and corn prices are the real tell.

items.title: October: S&P -0.93%, equal-weight +4.9%, Nasdaq -6.7%, a 5.6pt spread in one month
items.idea: S&P 500 closed October down 0.93% (+10.7% YTD, 11.8% with dividends). Equal-weight gained 4.9% and Nasdaq lost 6.7%. Callum notes the last five months are basically a range trade with cracks in the bull narrative.
items.angle: Leadership rotation inside a flat index. A single-month cap vs equal weight gap this wide is rare.
items.tweetA: Nasdaq -6.7%, equal-weight S&P +4.9%. Same month. The index went nowhere but the market underneath moved 11 points. If you only watch SPX you missed the biggest rotation of the year.
items.tweetB: Five months of range trading, +10.7% YTD, and the Nasdaq just fell 6.7% in a month. The 'range' is made of violent rotations that cancel out. Realized vol at the sector level is the story, index vol is the mask.

items.title: Betting markets price a Dem House and fairly high odds of a Dem Senate, historically the best 3-month post-election outcome
items.idea: Prediction markets give a very high chance of a Democratic House and fairly high odds of Democratic Senate. Per @MrMBrown, that outcome has historically produced the best 3-month post-election returns (none included a Trump factor). November is the best month on average and positive 69% of the time, but best vs worst Novembers span +11% to -11%, and 31% were negative.
items.angle: Gridlock trade plus seasonality plus Fed pause. Still a 31% chance of a down month, so not a free lunch.
items.tweetA: Divided government has historically given the best 3 months after midterms. Betting markets say it's coming. November positive 69% of the time. The setup is as consensus-bullish as it gets, which is exactly when 31% of Novembers go the other way.
items.tweetB: Prediction markets now do the work of the political-risk desk. If a Dem House is a 90% price, it's not a trade, it's a base case. The open question is whether tariffs survive a divided Congress. That's the real swing factor for $SPY.

items.title: Value stocks (VTV) at all-time highs after yields peaked in October
items.idea: Value stocks made new all-time highs following the largely yields-driven August/September correction, which reversed in October with the peak in bond yields (chart via @CalebFranzen).
items.angle: The rotation is a rates trade. If yields turn back up the value leg is the one that gives it back.
items.tweetA: $VTV at all-time highs the month yields peaked. Value isn't a style here, it's a duration trade. Falling yields lifted the cheap-and-boring while the long-duration Mags broke. That's inverted from every prior rate cycle.
items.tweetB: Value at highs, tech capex at records, and the Nasdaq down 6.7%. The market is paying for cash flow today over cash flow in 2030. First time in three years that rotation had macro cover.

items.title: Global earnings revision breadth at the top of its range: last times were early-90s, 2000, 2018, 2021
items.idea: The share of companies globally with expanding forward earnings is at multi-year highs, and cross-country earnings revisions breadth has surged to the top of its range. Callum notes global equities corrected after similar readings in the early 90s, 2000, 2018 and 2021, with exceptions in the early 2000s and post-2008 where it marked recovery. Late-cycle surges plus overheated sentiment are a bad sign.
items.angle: Good news priced in: positive revisions are a sentiment, not fundamental, signal at the extreme.
items.tweetA: Earnings revisions breadth is at a level that last showed up in 1990, 2000, 2018 and 2021. Three of those four were tops. The only exceptions were recoveries from recessions. We are not coming out of a recession.
items.tweetB: Analysts are most optimistic exactly when they have the least room to be surprised. Revisions breadth at the ceiling isn't bullish, it's a crowd-consensus gauge. I'd rather own the stocks where estimates are still too low.

charts.desc: Global earnings breadth; revision breadth across countries with historical tops

items.title: Tech capex now the dominant spender in the S&P 500, breaking records on multiple angles
items.idea: Topdown Charts Research shows tech capex hitting records and muscling out all other sectors to become the dominant spender in the S&P 500. Callum adds that earnings momentum is already rolling over from strong levels while US leading indicators point to a slowdown in 2027, which could stall the tech earnings theme.
items.angle: Capex as the S&P's largest cash outlay is a regime shift in how the index converts earnings into returns. Buybacks lose, capex wins.
items.tweetA: Tech capex is now the largest use of cash in the S&P 500. Not buybacks. Not dividends. The index went from returning cash to shareholders to reinvesting it in data centers. That's a venture-capital business model priced at an index multiple.
items.tweetB: Earnings momentum rolling over, leading indicators pointing to a 2027 slowdown, and capex still stepping up. If revenue growth lags the build by even two quarters, depreciation drags earnings right when the multiple needs them.

items.source: Weekly ChartStorm / Meb Faber & inverted S&P
items.title: Biggest stock by market cap historically a bad buy, but the modern era has a breakout in 'biggening'
items.idea: Meb Faber's juxtaposition: buying the largest stock by market cap has historically underperformed with occasional strong stretches, and many 'biggest of the big' have come and gone. The recent era shows a breakout in how large the top names have become. Callum also shows an inverted S&P chart that looks like a rounding bottom, as a perspective check.
items.angle: Concentration at record levels with a poor historical forward return for the #1 name.
items.tweetA: Buying the largest stock in the index has been a losing strategy on average. Today the largest stock is bigger relative to everything else than at any point in the series. That's either a new regime or the longest mean-reversion setup ever drawn.
items.tweetB: Flip any chart upside down and it looks like a buy. The inverted S&P rounding bottom is a good reminder: the pattern you see depends on which way you hold the paper. Anchor on cash flows, not chart shapes.

items.title: Despite October's Fed hesitation, Callum says policy remains on a tightening path; 5-factor stance Neutral
items.idea: Callum keeps expensive valuations + consensus bullish sentiment + heavy equity exposure = dangerous background risk. He notes policy is still on a tightening path despite the Fed hesitation in October. Overall US stock stance: Neutral, increasingly adverse risk backdrop with few supports left.
items.angle: Tightening bias plus peak earnings momentum is the setup where equity multiples carry all the risk.
items.tweetA: Policy is still tightening and the market is paying seasonality-adjusted multiples. The Fed paused one meeting and everyone heard a pivot. Pauses in a hiking cycle are not cuts.
items.tweetB: Valuation expensive, sentiment bullish, positioning heavy: that's three of five boxes ticked on a risk framework with the supports running out. The good news is all in the price. What's the bad-news hedge?

items.title: Largest crypto hack ever: $6.3B drained from Binance by North Korea-linked TraderTraitor; $2.7B frozen in 40 minutes
items.idea: After escalated US-Iran conflict, a $6.3B hack hit Binance, attributed to Lazarus-affiliated TraderTraitor. Tether and Circle froze about $2.7B within 40 minutes, the fastest response ever. Binance will cover all user funds. The author argues hack frequency is accelerating because of AI tools and lists security as the investment opportunity plus dip-buying setups.
items.angle: Stablecoin issuers have become de facto enforcement layers: freeze power is now a feature. Centralization trade-off for the DeFi crowd.
items.tweetA: $2.7B of a $6.3B hack frozen in 40 minutes. By Tether and Circle. That is the real news: the two biggest stablecoins can claw back stolen money faster than any court. The censorship-resistance debate just ended and the answer was 'no'.
items.tweetB: A state actor took $6.3B and the platform eats the loss. Binance's balance sheet just became the most important insurer in crypto. And AI-assisted attacks are only starting. Security tokens, audits, custody: who actually gets paid?

items.title: 'Escalated conflict between US and Iran' as backdrop for the weekend crypto drawdown
items.idea: The newsletter opens by framing the Binance hack as happening after escalated conflict between the US and Iran. No detail in the preview on oil or rates, but it links geopolitical stress to risk assets over the same window.
items.angle: Need a cross-check on oil, gold and USD moves for the US-Iran escalation. Preview gives no specifics.
items.tweetA: Crypto got a US-Iran escalation and a Lazarus-sized hack in the same week. Bitcoin is trading as a liquidity asset, not a hedge. When the war headline hits, it's the leveraged longs that get hurt first, not oil shorts.
items.tweetB: Geopolitical risk plus a state-sponsored hack: North Korea's best funding source and Iran's best distraction both run through the same chain. The attack surface and the sanction surface are the same thing.

items.title: Bitcoin holds above short-term holder cost basis, but the cushion is narrowing
items.idea: Adler notes BTC is above the short-term holder realized price and the recovery continues, but the distance above that level is shrinking. He says similar conditions in the past led to both gains and deep declines. Report is a $1,200/year paid product so numbers are not in the email.
items.angle: STH cost basis is the line between a recovery and a bull trap. With Binance hack risk, a break below would flip recent buyers to underwater.
items.tweetA: Bitcoin is above the short-term holder cost basis by a shrinking margin. Every recent buyer is near breakeven, which is when the weakest hands sell the first dip. A hack and a rate wobble and the whole cohort goes underwater at once.
items.tweetB: Same on-chain setup has produced both rallies and deep drawdowns. The signal isn't direction, it's fragility. A thin cushion means the next catalyst decides, and the Binance breach was the catalyst.
